prompt: The quarantine for laptop was added with `nft add`, and laptop still reached app:8080 and www:443. Why?
hint: Where does `add` put a rule?

choices.text: `nft add` stages the rule until the rule set is reloaded
choices.why: The rule was live at once; it was listed with a handle.

choices.text: It went to the end, below accepts that matched first
choices.why: Right. Handle 10 accepted the connection before handle 20 was read.

choices.text: A drop needs a higher priority than an accept to win
choices.why: Rules in a chain have no priority of their own; position decides.

choices.text: The address in the rule was mistyped, so it matched no packet
choices.why: It was laptop's address: moved up, the same rule counted 2 packets.

prompt: After the quarantine was moved to position 4 and laptop tried again, how many packets had its counter recorded?
hint: counter packets ...

prompt: Lesson 9's quarantine used `insert` with no position. What does that do that `insert … position 4` avoids?
hint: Which rule is at the very top of the chain?

choices.text: It puts the rule at the end of the chain, the same as `add`
choices.why: insert with no position puts it at the top.

choices.text: It replaces the rule that had handle 4
choices.why: position 4 puts the rule before handle 4; nothing is deleted.

choices.text: It lands above the established rule, cutting open connections
choices.why: Right. position 4 leaves open connections alone and stops every new one.

choices.text: It is refused, as a position is required in a chain that has rules
choices.why: nft accepts it; lesson 9 used it.

prompt: Which of these statements about the order of rules does the section support? Choose all that apply.
hint: First match, and what each packet costs.

choices.text: A rule below an accept that matches the same packet is not consulted for it
choices.why: Right. The first match decides.

choices.text: nft prints a warning when a new rule is shadowed
choices.why: It loads silently; the counter is what shows it.

choices.text: Rules matching most traffic belong near the top
choices.why: Right. Every packet walks the chain until something matches.

choices.text: A drop rule is read before any accept, wherever it sits
choices.why: Action does not reorder rules; the quarantine proved it.

choices.text: Long lists of addresses belong in a set
choices.why: Right. A set is looked up in one step.

prompt: The SSH rule was typed with `ip saddr 192.168.99.0/16`. What did the listing show nftables had stored?
hint: A /16 keeps two bytes.

choices.text: `192.168.99.0/24`, the segment that was meant
choices.why: nftables does not guess intent; it keeps the /16.

choices.text: `192.168.99.0/16`, exactly as it was typed
choices.why: It was rewritten to the network the mask describes.
Right. Normalised to the network it describes.

choices.text: No rule: nft refused an address with host bits set
choices.why: It loaded without a complaint.

prompt: Which cell of the matrix did the /16 rule break?
hint: laptop is on the staff LAN, 192.168.10.20.

choices.text: Internet to servers: SSH now open to remote
choices.why: remote's address is not in 192.168.0.0/16.

choices.text: Staff LAN to servers: any port now open
choices.why: The rule names tcp dport 22 and no other port.

choices.text: Management to servers: SSH now blocked
choices.why: The admins' segment is inside the /16, so it still matches.

choices.text: Staff LAN to servers: SSH now open
choices.why: Right. laptop reached app:22 and db:22.

prompt: A /16 prefix keeps the first ___ bytes of the address.
hint: 16 bits.

prompt: Why can no packet match `iifname eth0 oifname eth1 ip saddr 192.0.2.53 tcp dport 443`?
hint: Which zone does each part describe?

choices.text: It arrives from the internet, yet comes from dns in the DMZ
choices.why: Right. The interfaces and the address describe opposite ends.

choices.text: Port 443 is not allowed in a forward chain
choices.why: Ports are matched in forward all the time.

choices.text: An accept rule may not name both interfaces
choices.why: The staff rule, handle 10, names both.

choices.text: The `counter` keyword has to come before the interfaces
choices.why: The counter worked; it read 0 because nothing matched.

prompt: What is the rule that was meant for dns's updates?
hint: Swap the two interfaces.

choices.text: `iifname eth0 oifname eth1 ip daddr 192.0.2.53 tcp dport 443`
choices.why: That lets the internet reach dns on 443, a different flow.

choices.text: `iifname eth1 oifname eth1 ip saddr 192.0.2.53 tcp dport 443`
choices.why: The updates leave through eth0, towards the internet.

choices.text: `iifname eth0 oifname eth1 ip saddr 192.0.2.53 tcp sport 443`
choices.why: The interfaces are still backwards; the port was right.

choices.text: `iifname eth1 oifname eth0 ip saddr 192.0.2.53 tcp dport 443`
choices.why: Right. In from the DMZ, out to the internet.

prompt: Match each symptom to its usual cause.
hint: The table at the end of the section.

pairs.left: counter at 0, the traffic still passes
pairs.right: an accept above it matches first

pairs.left: counter at 0, the traffic is still dropped
counter climbing, but on the wrong traffic
pairs.right: a mask or port range wider than meant

right_distractors: the kernel rejected the rule at load time

prompt: How many bytes had the catch-all `drop everything else` counted after the database attempt?
hint: counter packets 1 bytes ...

prompt: Why did the finance rule count 0 packets while db:5432 stayed blocked?
hint: Look at what sits above it.

choices.text: 5432 is not the database's port
choices.why: It is; the rule never got the chance to match.

choices.text: It sits below a drop that has no conditions
choices.why: Right. That drop decides for every packet it sees.

choices.text: eth2 is the wrong interface for the staff LAN
choices.why: The staff rule uses eth2 and works.

choices.text: It lacks `ct state new`, so the first packet of a connection skips it
choices.why: Without it the rule matches any packet of the flow, the first included.

prompt: Which of these protect a rule set against rules added after a catch-all? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section names two cheap ones.

choices.text: Swap the final drop for a reject, so blocked attempts are seen
choices.why: A reject is still an unconditional verdict and hides what is below it.

choices.text: Keep the rule set in a file and write new rules above its last line
choices.why: Right. The catch-all is visibly last there.

choices.text: Add rules with `nft add`, so the newest is easy to find at the end
choices.why: Appending is exactly how the finance rule got lost.

choices.text: Let the policy give the final verdict, and end with a rule that counts and decides nothing
choices.why: Right. A counting rule hides no rule below it.

prompt: Why does matrix-test.sh print a cell only when its result differs from the expected one?
hint: Picture a matrix of two hundred cells.

choices.text: probe reports blocked cells and no open ones
choices.why: probe reports both; matrix.expected has both.

choices.text: Printing each cell would take longer than probing it
choices.why: Ten cells take a few seconds either way.

choices.text: Passing cells would bury the failing one
choices.why: Right. Silence means the matrix holds.

choices.text: The exit code is set from the length of the output
choices.why: It is set by the fail variable.

prompt: How many cells does the lesson's matrix.expected list?
hint: One line per cell.

prompt: Run against the rule set with the /16 mistake, which line did the test print?
hint: Which cells in matrix.expected involve port 22?

choices.text: `admin app:22 expected open got blocked`
choices.why: admin is inside the /16, so its SSH stayed open.

choices.text: `laptop app:22 expected blocked got open`
choices.why: Right. The one cell the wide mask opened.

choices.text: `laptop db:22 expected blocked got open`
choices.why: db:22 did open, but matrix.expected has no such cell to try.

choices.text: `laptop db:5432 expected blocked got open`
choices.why: The rule names port 22, not the database's port.

prompt: Put the steps of a rule change guarded by the matrix test in order.
hint: The test checks what is loaded.
items: write the change into the rule-set file
trap: Running the test before loading tests the old rule set, and passes whatever the change does.

prompt: Why does each line of the test start its probe on the machine named in the first column?
hint: What do the rules match on?

choices.text: The firewall logs connections from the lab host alone
choices.why: Logging is not what is being tested.

choices.text: probe needs the target's name resolved in that zone's DNS
choices.why: Names are not the point; the path through the firewall is.

choices.text: It keeps the test quicker than trying each cell from one place
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; from one place, most cells would test the wrong path.

choices.text: Rules match interfaces and sources of the zone it starts in
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the test tries a different path from the one in the cell.

prompt: A rule is added so that www stops reaching a mail relay on port 25. After www tries, the rule's counter reads 0 and the mail still goes through. What is the likeliest cause?
hint: Zero, and the traffic passes.

choices.text: The rule is written the wrong way round
choices.why: Then nothing would accept it either; the traffic would still be dropped by the policy.

choices.text: An accept above it matches first
choices.why: Right. Counter at 0 and traffic passing is a shadowed rule.

choices.text: Its mask is wider than intended
choices.why: A wide mask makes a counter climb, on too much traffic.

choices.text: It was appended below a final catch-all drop
choices.why: The catch-all would have dropped the mail, and it passed.

a block appended beneath a broader accept

prompt: A router ACL meant for 10.1.5.0/24 was typed with the wildcard 0.0.255.255. How many /24 networks does the line now match?
hint: One wrong byte.

prompt: On the baseline, laptop is quarantined with the rule at position 4, and matrix.expected is left as it was. What does matrix-test.sh print?
hint: Which cells start on laptop, and what do they expect?

choices.text: Silence, and exit 0, as the quarantine is intended
choices.why: The file still expects laptop app:8080 open; the test knows no intent.

choices.text: `laptop app:22 expected blocked got open`
choices.why: That was the /16 mistake; the baseline has none.

choices.text: Three lines, one per laptop cell
choices.why: app:22 and db:5432 were expected blocked and are blocked; they match.

choices.text: `laptop app:8080 expected open got blocked`, and exit 1
choices.why: Right. A deliberate change needs matrix.expected changed with it.
